section_summary: This section follows negotiations between foreign oil companies and Japanese officials over quotas, required oil stocks, refining permits, and prices under the 1934 Petroleum Industry Law. It contains the companies’ proposed memorandum, a detailed conversation record, the Japanese Commerce Department’s draft reply, and subsequent diplomatic reporting. By early March 1935, talks had been suspended until after the Diet session, with the foreign companies considering withdrawal if the rules were not changed.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, conclusion of despatch No. 1168
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a dispute over Yoshino’s draft reply, renewed talks, 1935 quotas, and Japan’s search for foreign oil fields.
subfiles.summary: A threatening oral message accompanying Yoshino’s reply was later softened, allowing talks to resume on February 7. The despatch reviews quota allocations that favored Japanese refiners while granting foreign importers part of anticipated growth. It also reports Japanese interest in oil fields in Mexico, Peru, and Colombia.

subfiles.title: Draft memorandum to the Ministry of Commerce
subfiles.from: Standard-Vacuum Oil Company and Rising Sun Petroleum Company
subfiles.to: Japanese Ministry of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: Sets out foreign importers’ objections and requested assurances under the Petroleum Industry Law.
subfiles.summary: The companies seek a durable share of gasoline trade and proportional treatment of increases and decreases in consumption. They contest the cost of mandatory oil storage, question the economics of expanded local refining, and request a price formula covering importers’ costs and a reasonable profit. Exhibits compare international refinery capacity and project Japanese gasoline demand.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation at Tokyo Club, January 30, 1935
subfiles.from: Foreign oil company representatives and Japanese officials
subfiles.about: Records a detailed discussion of the companies’ draft memorandum and the administration of the oil law.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino and Kurusu discuss quota principles, idle refinery capacity, treatment of Korea and Taiwan, storage costs, refining permits, and price calculations with company representatives. Yoshino rejects a guaranteed market percentage but privately suggests sharing future growth equally after idle capacity is filled. The companies press for written assurances and argue that the stock requirement and controlled prices threaten their ability to continue operating.

subfiles.title: Reply of the Department of Commerce and Industry to foreign oil companies
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: Rejects the companies’ memorandum as written and states the department’s positions on quotas, storage, refining, and prices.
subfiles.summary: The department declines to guarantee trade by percentage and gives local refiners preference while unused capacity remains. It rules out subsidies or postponing storage requirements, though it promises lenient application. It also declines to fix permanent price formula rates.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning the Japanese Control Law
subfiles.about: Relays a proposed Japanese press statement and explains why foreign oil representatives are leaving Japan temporarily.
subfiles.summary: The letter says negotiations have stalled and Japanese officials have retreated from earlier positions. Company representatives plan to return in April after officials establish their authority to make commitments.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Tokyo telegram No. 44
subfiles.about: Recommends against separately notifying Dundas of Tokyo’s March 2 telegram.
subfiles.summary: The division concludes that Standard-Vacuum already knows the material developments and can form its own assessment.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 44 on American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports suspension of oil talks and Hirota’s response to an informal diplomatic approach.
subfiles.summary: Foreign representatives are departing for Manila and expect to resume talks after the Diet session. They remain dissatisfied with officials’ retreat from oral understandings but have not decided whether to threaten withdrawal. Hirota hopes for an agreement after adjournment and acknowledges Japan’s dependence on American oil.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Tokyo despatch No. 1182
subfiles.about: Comments on despatch No. 1182 and Japanese proposals for foreign firms to associate with Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: The writer questions Dickover’s view that such associations usually disadvantage American firms, citing Geary’s experience.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch No. 1182
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports deteriorating prospects in the continuing talks and introduces two enclosed conversation records.
subfiles.summary: A revised company memorandum addresses future business assurances, oil stocks, quotas, and prices, but the Japanese position has hardened. Foreign representatives are increasingly pessimistic. The enclosures discuss both the negotiations and Kurusu’s suggestion that the companies obtain Japanese capital or influential advisers.

subfiles.title: Neville conversation with Parker and Goold
subfiles.about: Records company discussions of the Manchukuo oil monopoly and possible outcomes of negotiations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Parker and Goold describe an approach concerning crude oil sales to the Manchukuo monopoly and seek advice on the status of assurances from Japanese officials. Neville explains the limits of any reply Yoshino and Kurusu could give before consulting other departments. The representatives consider setting a minimum selling price or withdrawing if no satisfactory agreement emerges.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Kurusu, Sansom, and Dickover
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s suggestions for improving foreign oil companies’ access to Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu attributes part of the companies’ difficulties to language barriers and weak connections in Tokyo. He suggests Japanese investors or influential Japanese advisers. Sansom and Dickover oppose shared ownership, while the participants discuss several possible advisers.

subfiles.title: Document file note on oil situation in Japan
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Knabenshue letter about a conversation with Lord Stanhope on oil supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Points to a separate letter discussing British-American cooperation and possible restriction of oil and capital supplies.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan, despatch No. 1193
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reviews the breakdown and postponement of oil negotiations, diplomatic representations, and attempts to secure crude oil supplies.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials reject parts of the companies’ February memorandum and seek time to consult other departments after the Diet session. Grew describes possible changes to stock requirements, the companies’ price and quota demands, and their contemplated warning of withdrawal. He reports his informal approach to Hirota, efforts to restrict Japan’s access to new crude sources, and his view that agreement may still be possible when talks resume.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Kurusu, Neville, and Sansom, February 25
subfiles.about: Records Kurusu’s objection to the preamble of the companies’ draft memorandum and his oral assurances.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says a written claim that Yoshino accepts the memorandum would embarrass him with other departments. He assures Neville and Sansom that the memorandum will guide further talks, while declining to bind himself or Yoshino on details. The conversation continues beyond page 148.
